passage:
Sonali was only a final-year student, but as the teaching assistant for the first-year coding lab in Pune, she had noticed Vijay: front row, writing down everything she said, even her jokes. Lately he messaged her at night. "Didi, should I take the robotics club or the debate club?" "Which laptop should I buy?" "Is my code okay?"
It was flattering. It was also a lot.
On Thursday he offered eagerly, "Didi, I can make your lab slides for you if you want." She could have used the help. She thought about it for a second, and said no. It wouldn't be fair to take his time just because he looked up to her.
After lab she sat with him. "You ask me everything. I like helping. But I don't know robotics, and I'm wrong about laptops all the time. Try deciding the club yourself, then tell me why."
He looked crestfallen, then thoughtful.
Next week he messaged: "Joined robotics. Reason: I like building. Is that a good reason?" She replied, "Your reason. Good enough."

qa.q: What did Vijay offer to do for Sonali?
qa.a: Make her lab slides.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about Vijay's constant messages?
qa.a: Flattered, but also overwhelmed by how much he leaned on her.

qa.q: How did Sonali guide Vijay without creating dependence?
qa.a: She admitted her limits, refused to use his admiration for favours, and asked him to choose the club himself and explain why.

qa.q: How does Vijay see Sonali?
qa.a: As someone to follow and ask about everything; he looks crestfallen when she steps back, then thoughtful.

grounding: Shows being looked up to by a junior and guiding him without creating dependence or using his admiration for favours.

"Jaya di, you're literally my role model," Nandini said, perching on the lab stool. "I even changed my specialisation because of your talk."
Jaya laughed, a bit uneasily. "Please tell me you had other reasons."
"Some. Mostly you." Nandini grinned. "Also, I can do your survey data entry. Anytime. For free."
Jaya looked at the four hundred forms stacked on her desk. It would save her a week. "That's kind. But no. You'd be doing it because you like me, not because it helps you learn."
"But I want to."
"Then do something for you. Professor Menon's lab needs a volunteer for real analysis work. Apply yourself. I'll tell you what I know, which honestly isn't much about her group."
"You think I'd get it?"
"I think you should find out without me in the middle."
Nandini hesitated. "Will you still read my application?"
"Once. Then it's yours."

qa.q: How many forms were stacked on Jaya's desk?
qa.a: Four hundred.

qa.q: Why did Jaya laugh a bit uneasily?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable that Nandini had changed specialisation mostly because of her, sensing too much weight placed on her.

qa.q: How did Jaya avoid using Nandini's admiration?
qa.a: She declined the free data entry, pointed Nandini to a real opportunity to apply for herself, was honest about her limited knowledge, and agreed to read the application only once.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Jaya?
qa.a: As a role model to follow closely, eager to help her and reluctant to act without her.

grounding: Illustrates being admired by a younger student and choosing honesty about one's limits and her independence over free favours.

He had a reputation for sending students out over late assignments, so I skipped his office hours and hoped it would click on its own. It didn't. My first quiz came back at 4 out of 20.
That scared me more than he did. So on Monday I wrote down exactly where I was stuck, three examples, page numbers, and went at 4 p.m.
He was eating a banana. He had a small plant on his desk and a photo of a dog. He listened, drew one diagram, and said, "Everyone gets lost at transfer functions. Come every Monday until you don't."
I've gone five Mondays now. I got 14 on the second quiz. He's still strict. He's also a person who named his dog Resistor.
— Vikas

qa.a: 4 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Vikas avoid Dr. Sharma's office hours at first?
qa.a: Vikas was scared of Dr. Sharma's strict reputation and hoped the subject would click without help.

qa.q: What did Vikas do to make the visit work?
qa.a: Wrote down exactly where the confusion was, with three examples and page numbers, and went to office hours on Monday.

qa.q: How does Dr. Sharma see Vikas's struggle?
qa.a: As normal ("Everyone gets lost at transfer functions"), and he invites Vikas to come every Monday.

grounding: Shows fear of a strict professor, the cost of avoiding him, and preparing, going to office hours and finding him human.

Academic advisor's note, MSc first year, 11 October
Neelam has missed two thesis check-ins with Prof. Vinita Kulkarni. Today she came to me instead, pale, saying she was "too scared to face her now" because the delay had grown so long. She admitted she had been avoiding the department corridor for three weeks.
I asked what she was afraid of. "That she'll say I'm not serious." I pointed out that each missed week made that more likely, not less.
We prepared together: a one-page summary of what she had done, where she was stuck, and a realistic new timeline. I suggested she open with an apology, not excuses.
At 3 p.m. I walked with her as far as the professor's door and waited in the corridor. She came out twenty minutes later, flushed but smiling. "She said, 'Next time, come when you're stuck, not when you've finished being scared.'" They have fixed weekly Tuesday meetings.

qa.a: That Prof. Kulkarni would think she wasn't serious; she was pale and too scared to face her.

qa.q: How did the advisor help Neelam face the professor?
qa.a: By preparing a one-page summary, stuck points and a new timeline with her, suggesting an apology instead of excuses, and walking her to the door.

qa.q: How does Prof. Kulkarni respond to Neelam?
qa.a: Firmly but kindly, telling her to come when stuck and setting weekly Tuesday meetings.

grounding: Illustrates avoiding a strict professor until the problem grows, and preparing and going to see her with support.

You know I worshipped Dr. Nirmala Pillai, Anju. In first year she's the reason I chose microbiology. She'd stay late explaining plating techniques; she lent me her own lab coat.
Then last month, in the lab meeting, she tore apart Revathi's presentation in front of everyone, and later I heard her say it was because Revathi had "sided with the other group" in some department quarrel. Petty. Really petty. And I realised she'd been giving the good projects to the people who flattered her.
For a week I was so angry I wanted to quit research. I told my roommate all professors are the same, just politics.
But then I was setting up a plate, and my hands did it exactly the way she taught me: careful, sterile, no shortcuts. That skill is real. It's mine now.
So I'm keeping the technique and dropping the pedestal. And I'm not giving up on every teacher because of one. I'm Keerthana, still a microbiologist, just less starry-eyed.

qa.q: What did Dr. Pillai lend Keerthana in first year?
qa.a: Her own lab coat.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after the lab meeting?
qa.a: Angry and disillusioned, wanting to quit research and calling all professors "just politics".

qa.q: What did Keerthana decide to keep, and what to let go?
qa.a: To keep the careful technique Dr. Pillai taught, drop the pedestal, and not turn cynical about every teacher.

qa.q: How might Revathi have experienced the lab meeting?
qa.a: As humiliating and unfair, torn apart in front of everyone over a department quarrel.

grounding: Shows discovering that a mentor is petty and biased, keeping what she taught while updating one's view instead of rejecting all authority.

qa.a: Unfairly passed over after beating both debaters in trials, and probably discouraged.

Anders had drafted the email to Professor Hana Berg six times. The master's application in Copenhagen was due in five weeks, and he needed a letter. He had taken two of her courses and worked on one research project, but she taught two hundred students a year. What if she didn't remember him?

Instead he wrote: "Dear Professor Berg, I'm applying to the Environmental Science master's in Copenhagen, due 15 March. I took your Soil Ecology course and worked on the wetland sampling project with your group last spring. Would you feel able to write a recommendation? I've attached my CV, a short summary of my project work and my draft statement. If it isn't possible, I completely understand."
He sent it at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday. By lunch she had replied: "Of course I remember the wetland data; your field notes were the tidiest in the group. Happy to write. Thank you for giving me time."

qa.q: What worried Anders about asking Professor Berg?
qa.a: He feared she wouldn't remember him among two hundred students a year, which made him anxious about asking.

qa.q: What made Anders's request a good one?
qa.a: He asked five weeks early and politely, reminded her of his course and project, attached his CV, summary and statement, and made it easy for her to say no.

qa.q: How did Professor Berg feel about the request?
qa.a: Pleased; she remembered his tidy field notes and thanked him for giving her time.

grounding: Shows worrying about asking for a recommendation, and asking early and politely with context about one's work.

At the civil engineering firm in Chennai, Uday had a habit: whenever a problem came up on the site drawings, he walked to Sudha ma'am's desk. "Ma'am, what should I do?" In three months he had asked her about beam sizes, email wording, and once, where to eat lunch.
On Thursday she didn't look up from her screen. "Uday, before you ask me anything today, bring me two options and which one you'd choose."
He went back to his desk, irritated, and stared at the drainage problem. Slowly he sketched one fix, then another. The second was cheaper but meant rerouting a pipe. He wrote down why he'd pick it.
At four he returned. "Option A, option B. I'd go with B because..."
She listened, asked one question he hadn't thought of, and nodded. "Good. Adjust for that and send it."
Walking back, he felt taller than he had in weeks. The next morning he solved a smaller problem without going to her at all.

qa.a: Beam sizes, email wording, and once, where to eat lunch.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when Sudha ma'am asked for two options?
qa.a: Irritated at first, then, after presenting his own choice, proud and taller than he had felt in weeks.

qa.q: What habit did Sudha ma'am's request build?
qa.a: Bringing his own options and a recommendation, which grew his judgement until he solved the next problem alone.

grounding: Shows waiting for a mentor to decide everything, and growing into independent judgement by bringing one's own ideas.

passage:
In her first month at the newspaper office on Park Street, Sharmila followed Irfan everywhere. He was the senior crime reporter who had broken the hospital fire story, and she wanted to be exactly him: the worn satchel, the three pens, the habit of calling sources from the stairwell.
When Irfan mentioned he had once left a full-time job to freelance, she started drafting her own resignation.
He found the draft on the shared printer. "Sharmila. Why?"
"Because it worked for you."
He sat her down in the canteen. "I left because my editor then was killing stories. Yours isn't. You'd be copying my decision without my reason." He pushed his notebook towards her. "Copy this instead. How I check a fact three ways before I file. How I listen to what a source doesn't say."
She read his notes for an hour. Then she shredded the draft. The next week she filed her first story, on school buses, a beat he had never covered, checked three ways.

qa.q: Which story had Irfan broken?
qa.a: The hospital fire story.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila start drafting a resignation?
qa.a: She admired Irfan so much that she wanted to copy his choice to freelance simply because it had worked for him.

qa.q: What did Irfan tell Sharmila to learn from him instead?
qa.a: His thinking: checking a fact three ways and listening to what a source doesn't say, not his personal decisions.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel on finding the draft?
qa.a: Concerned; he saw she was copying his decision without his reason and took the time to explain.

grounding: Illustrates admiring a senior and learning his way of thinking instead of imitating his choices while ignoring one's own path.
